870.bp: When you shop online, the product information you see—photos, descriptions, prices, categories—comes from a catalog. That catalog is only useful if it's accurate and complete. For large retailers selling thousands of items, keeping all that data clean and consistent is exhausting work, and mistakes slip through. This paper asks: can an AI system fix those mistakes automatically, by comparing a retailer's messy catalog against a brand's clean reference data?
870.wh: The obvious approach would be to fix each product entry in isolation: find mistakes in one row, correct them, then move to the next. But real-world catalogs are tangled; a single product might have the wrong category *and* missing attributes *and* a typo in the name all at once. Fixing them one at a time means you might correct the category, then realize the typo actually implies the category was half-right. You need to see the whole picture.
870.wh2: The paper says prior methods "usually repair and match product entries separately." That's the rub: they handle the data-cleaning step and the data-matching step sequentially, as if they're independent problems. But they're not. You can't know if an entry truly matches a reference until you've cleaned the entry.
870.ap: This work uses two things together: a large language model (a machine that reads and reasons about text) and a brand's knowledge base (a clean, structured list of product definitions). The LLM acts as an agent—a worker that can follow instructions, read messy data, consult the reference, and make decisions. The key move is that it does both repair *and* matching at the same time. Instead of fixing the entry, then searching for a match, it reasons about what the entry should be *while* finding which reference product it belongs to.
870.ww: When you try to match a messy product entry to a clean reference, both cleaning and matching inform each other. An LLM can hold both problems in mind: "This entry has a typo and a wrong category, so when I look for the matching reference product, I should ignore those noise signals and focus on what's actually being described." Doing them concurrently means the LLM can course-correct itself as it learns more.
870.po: The paper shows this approach actually works—it improves the quality of large product catalogs automatically. For e-commerce, this means customers see accurate, complete product pages, which boosts trust and click-through rates. For retailers, it means less manual data cleanup and fewer customer complaints about wrong shipping or mismatched descriptions.

871.bp: Recommendation systems are everywhere: Netflix suggests shows, Spotify suggests songs, Amazon suggests products. But most recommendation systems have a blind spot: they're obsessed with popular items because those get the most clicks and sales. Unpopular but really good items—indie movies, niche music, specialized tools—almost never surface. This paper tackles that unfairness: how do you make recommendations that surface hidden gems, not just blockbusters?
871.wh: The core tension is that popularity and quality are not the same thing. A recommendation system trained on who-clicks-what will learn that popular items get clicked a lot, so it learns to recommend them constantly. But many users would actually prefer something less mainstream if they knew it existed. The problem gets worse the more unpopular an item is: the system has less data about it, so it's less confident, and confidence is often how systems rank candidates. Result: long-tail items stay invisible.
871.ap: SAGERec builds a representation (a compressed summary) of each user based on two signals: the user's own data and the data from the most informative items they've actually clicked. The trick is identifying which items are "most informative." Instead of picking them with a hard rule, the paper trains a separate neural network to learn which items matter most—a learner learning what to pay attention to. Then they use two expert sub-models that each score items differently, and a gating mechanism (a learned decision-maker) that blends those scores based on whether an item is from the long tail or not.
871.ww: Why does this help? First, focusing on the most informative items means you're not drowned in noise from items the user clicked-but-didn't-really-care-about. Second, training separate experts for tail vs. popular items means each can be optimized for its regime. The gating mechanism then acts as a kind of traffic cop: for long-tail items, it trusts the tail-specialist expert more. This breaks the feedback loop where popular items get recommended more because they're popular.
871.po: Experiments on real datasets show SAGERec recommends long-tail items much better than older systems while staying competitive on popular items. The concrete payoff: users discover items that match their taste but aren't trending, which makes their experience richer and supports creators of niche content.

872.bp: Misinformation spreads fast online. Fact-checking is the counterforce: journalists and tools verify whether a claim is true. But fact-checking is hard because claims are often complex. A single sentence might assert three things at once: "This policy was passed in 2019 and raised unemployment in rural areas by 3%." You have to check each piece, and those pieces often depend on each other—you can't verify "rural unemployment rose" without first knowing whether the policy actually passed.
872.wh: Recent fact-checking systems use large language models and break complex claims into simpler sub-claims to check each one. That's smart: it's easier for a machine to verify "The policy passed" than to verify the whole sentence at once. But the gap is that these systems treat each sub-claim as independent. They never ask: "Does the answer to sub-claim #2 change what sub-claim #3 means?" For claims that need you to follow a chain of reasoning (multi-hop reasoning), that's catastrophic. You verify each link of the chain in isolation, and miss contradictions between links.
872.ap: This paper proposes DagFC (Dependency-Aware Fact-Checking). Instead of breaking the claim into sub-claims at random, it builds a knowledge graph—a map showing which sub-claims depend on which others. For instance, if checking "the policy passed" is needed before checking "unemployment rose," the graph captures that dependency. Then, the system verifies sub-claims in an order that respects those dependencies. When it finishes verifying one, it uses that result to guide the verification of the next, carrying intermediate findings forward. The term "dag" refers to the shape of that dependency map (a directed acyclic graph).
872.ww: The first-principles reason this works: humans do multi-hop reasoning by keeping intermediate conclusions in mind and using them to check the next step. "The policy passed *in 2019*, so I should check unemployment data *from 2019 onwards*." By encoding dependencies, the system mimics that practice. It also avoids verifying the same sub-claim twice; if "the policy passed" has already been verified, the next sub-claim can reuse that verdict instead of re-checking from scratch.
872.po: The concrete payoff: complex claims with multi-hop reasoning get verified more accurately because the system respects the logical structure. This means fact-checking tools can handle the trickiest claims—the ones bad actors craft precisely to confuse simple, step-by-step verification.

873.bp: Imagine a ride-sharing app that doesn't just get you from A to B, but that learns *why* you chose that route. Maybe you took the scenic route because you wanted fresh air, or you chose a neighborhood because you heard it had a cool vibe. The real goal is moving beyond "Where do people go?" to "Why do people feel drawn to places?" This paper builds a system to collect that sensory and emotional data at scale, so future recommendations can consider not just popularity, but how a place *feels*.
873.wh: Existing recommendation systems for places (maps, ride-sharing, tourism apps) rely on reviews and ratings, which are text-based signals. But whether a place appeals to you depends on subtler, multisensory things: Is it noisy? Does it smell fresh? Are the colors pleasing? Is it crowded? These nuances are almost impossible to capture in a review text. And different people react differently to the same sensory input depending on their personality—someone who seeks thrills might love a loud, chaotic market; someone who seeks calm might hate it. Standard systems don't model that.
873.ap: The paper presents FreePOST, a location-based app where users submit photos along with tags describing their sensory experience (noisy, crowded, calm, vibrant, etc.) tied to specific places. Over three months in Kyoto, 69 people contributed over 8,000 posts. The system also collected personality data using standard psychology questionnaires (Big Five Inventory, Sensation Seeking Scale) so that the sensory impressions could be paired with who reported them. The data is visualized on an interactive map in real time.
873.ww: The insight is straightforward: sensory experience of a place is real and varies by observer. By collecting both the sensory tags *and* the personality profile of who tagged it, the system can later learn patterns like "people high in openness love vibrant, crowded places" or "people low in extraversion avoid noisy locations." This is the data foundation for personalized recommendations that consider how a place fits a person's sensory and temperamental preferences, not just the average rating.
873.po: This data collection provides a foundation for future location recommendation and mobility services that feel more human. Instead of recommending the "best-reviewed" place, a system could recommend places that match a user's personality and preferred sensory experience. The concrete payoff is captured in the paper: a foundation for "personalized search and recommendation in MaaS contexts"—meaning ride-sharing and mobility apps can eventually recommend routes and destinations that suit the person, not just the destination's average popularity.

874.bp: When you ask a smart assistant a question in the middle of a conversation, the assistant needs to find the right answer in a massive database of interconnected concepts and facts. A knowledge graph is a structured database where information is represented as connected nodes: "Barack Obama" (a person) is connected to "2008" (a year) which is connected to "U.S. Presidential Election" (an event). The challenge is: how do you find the right node when the question is messy, contextual, and embedded in a multi-turn conversation?
874.wh: The obvious approach: translate the user's question into a search query, find matching nodes, rank them by some score. But that misses context. If the user previously asked about "U.S. elections," and now asks "Who won in 2008?", the context matters. Also, a single answer node ("Barack Obama") is surrounded by a neighborhood of related nodes ("Democratic Party," "Illinois," "Hope"), and different searches might care about different neighbors. A naive system that only looks at whether "Barack Obama" lexically matches the question might miss it entirely if the question uses synonyms.
874.ap: DRAGON (Diverse Relevance signal Aggregation via Graph cONvolution) takes a different approach. For each candidate answer node, it first builds a sub-graph—a small map of the candidate, its neighbors, and their connections. Then, it computes many fine-grained relevance signals: How well does the current turn of the conversation match the candidate node's name? How well does it match its neighbors? What about previous turns? All these signals are represented as sparse vectors (lists of numbers). DRAGON then uses graph convolution—a neural technique that propagates signals through the sub-graph—to blend and transform all these signals together, eventually producing a ranking score for that candidate.
874.ww: The reason this works: different parts of the sub-graph are relevant at different moments in the conversation. By propagating signals through the graph, the system can learn that "Obama" is relevant because the candidate node itself matches, but also because its neighbors (Democratic Party, 2008) match previous turns. Graph convolution naturally captures these multi-hop relationships. By explicitly representing many fine-grained signals (not just one score), the system also has more information to work with, reducing the chance it misses a good answer.
874.po: The payoff is better entity retrieval in conversational systems. When you ask a multi-turn question about a knowledge graph, the system finds the right node more often, leading to smarter, more contextual answers from voice assistants, chatbots, and other conversational systems.

875.bp: Misinformation spreads online because people believe it. Understanding why people believe false claims is the first step to stopping the spread. Unlike systems that only analyze the text of false claims (does it sound true?), this paper flips the lens: it asks what linguistic features actually *predict* whether people will find something believable, and it does so by analyzing real human judgments from social media discussions.
875.wh: Most misinformation detection systems work backwards. They assume a claim is true or false, then try to detect which is which using facts, sources, or the text's logical consistency. But that's not how humans judge credibility. Humans read a claim and feel an intuitive sense of whether to trust it, based on cues in the language itself. A sentence with clear verbs and specific dates feels more credible than a vague one. Proper nouns feel more credible than pronouns. This intuition can be wrong, but it's powerful. Systems that only look at factual accuracy miss what actually persuades people.
875.ap: The paper analyzed real social-media discussions where people posted claims and others voted on whether they believed them. It collected both the human believability judgments *and* linguistic features of the claims: which verbs were used, whether proper nouns appeared, the emotional tone, the sentence structure. It also collected user features: the commenter's personality proxies (inferred from their writing), their engagement level, their tone. Then it trained a graph neural network (a type of model good at learning from interconnected data) to predict believability from those signals, encoding both the linguistic features and user features as edge properties in a social graph.
875.ww: Why does this work? Because people's judgment of credibility depends on both the text and who's saying it. A claim about politics written by someone with a history of political engagement feels more credible than the same claim from someone who rarely engages. And certain linguistic patterns—mixing emotional and contradictory cues (what the paper calls "ambivalence")—are correlated with deception. By modeling both together in a graph, the system captures how credibility is a product of both message and messenger.
875.po: The concrete payoff: misinformation detection improves when you model human credibility judgments alongside linguistic signals. The paper shows that incorporating believability signals as features improves detection substantially over text-only systems. The deeper payoff is insight: the paper reveals domain-specific linguistic markers—politics uses emotion-cognition tension, entertainment uses sentiment mixing—suggesting that deception has recognizable patterns.

876.bp: When you click an ad on your phone or see a product recommendation, a system somewhere predicted whether you'd click on it. That's click-through rate (CTR) prediction. For advertisers and e-commerce sites, even a 1% improvement in accuracy translates to millions of dollars in revenue. CTR prediction relies on learning patterns in user behavior from past clicks. The challenge: as data grows, how do you build models that efficiently capture many different kinds of click patterns at once?
876.wh: Modern CTR systems use parallel architectures—imagine multiple parallel pipelines, each specialized for a different kind of pattern. One pipeline might capture gender-based patterns, another price-sensitive patterns, another seasonal patterns. But there are two problems. First, all pipelines typically start with the same base features (mathematical descriptions of user history, item features, etc.), so they're not truly specialized—they see the same input, so they can't learn truly different signals. Second, as you stack more layers (attempting to capture complex, multi-way patterns between features), each layer can introduce errors that propagate downstream, degrading the final prediction.
876.ap: DGNet (Decoupled Gated Network) solves this in two parts. First, a Decoupled Embedding Generator creates pipeline-specific versions of each input feature. Instead of all pipelines using the same representation of "user age," the generator creates a version optimized for the gender-pattern pipeline, another for the price-pattern pipeline, etc. Second, a Gated Fusion Module dynamically picks out the most useful signal from each layer of each pipeline before it propagates to the next layer. It's like a filter: "Layer 1 of the price-pipeline has learned a useful signal, but layer 1 of the gender-pipeline is just amplifying noise, so reduce its contribution going forward."
876.ww: Decoupling embeddings means each pipeline can learn the signal it's specialized for without interference from other pipelines' noise. The gating mechanism prevents error accumulation: instead of letting all signals propagate unchanged through layers, it learns to dampen weak or noisy signals and amplify clean ones. This is especially important for CTR prediction, where the majority of instances are non-clicks (you don't click 99% of ads), so noise can easily dominate the signal.
876.po: The result: DGNet consistently improves the performance of existing parallel CTR models, statistically significantly, with the same basic architecture. This is valuable because it's "model-agnostic"—you can add it to systems already deployed. The concrete payoff for advertising and e-commerce: better click prediction means better ad placement and more relevant recommendations, which improves user experience and platform revenue.

877.bp: Large language models like ChatGPT and PaLM are trained on huge amounts of text scraped from the internet. But the internet isn't neutral; it's written by humans with opinions, biases, and blind spots. This paper asks a straightforward question: Does the internet text reflect political bias, and if so, does that bias leak into the language models trained on it? Understanding this is crucial because biased models can mislead users or reinforce false beliefs at scale.
877.wh: Most studies of bias in language models look at the model's outputs directly ("Does it generate left-leaning or right-leaning text?"). But that's after-the-fact diagnosis. The harder, more fundamental question is whether the bias *originates* in the training data. Few studies have done large-scale analysis of political bias in web text itself. The C4 corpus is a 700 billion token dataset of web text used to train T5, PaLM, and LaMDA—flagship models. If the corpus is biased, those models probably are too. But proving that requires carefully annotating thousands of pages for political stance and running statistical tests to rule out random variation.
877.ap: The paper analyzed 15 politically sensitive topics (gender equality, LGBTQ rights, abortion, economic policy, etc.) in the C4 corpus. They used an LLM itself to annotate each page from multiple political perspectives ("How would a progressive person evaluate this?" "A libertarian?"), then validated those annotations with rigorous statistical tests (equivalence testing, multiple testing correction, so false positives are ruled out). They also ran experiments correlating corpus-level bias with the output of models trained on that corpus, and tested whether fine-tuning could reduce the model's bias.
877.ww: The mechanism is straightforward: if text A contains more left-leaning content than text B, a language model trained on A will statistically predict left-leaning next-tokens more often. The LLM doesn't have values; it's just learned from the data distribution. So corpus bias flows directly into model behavior. The paper provides evidence for this by showing correlations between corpus-level bias and model output bias.
877.po: The paper reveals clear patterns: the C4 corpus has left-leaning, supportive bias on social and cultural topics (gender equality, LGBTQ, abortion) while economic topics are more balanced. This bias propagates into models. The concrete payoff is twofold: (1) awareness that major language models carry these biases, and (2) empirical evidence that the root cause is the training data, not the model architecture, which opens the door to better data curation or filtering as a mitigation strategy.

878.bp: When you search for something, your initial query is often vague or incomplete. "Machine learning libraries" is better than "ML," but even better would be "Python machine learning libraries for computer vision that are easy to learn." Query expansion fixes this: instead of searching for your exact words, the system supplements your query with related concepts, so it retrieves documents you actually need, not just documents with your keywords. The challenge is making that expansion rich and diverse, not narrow and repetitive.
878.wh: Recent systems use large language models to do query expansion: you give an LLM your query and it generates pseudo-documents (made-up content that's relevant to the query). Those are added to the search. But LLMs tend to stay in a narrow lane. They generate content that's closely similar to the original query, missing the broader context or diverse angles that a human might consider. For example, expanding "climate change solutions" might generate many documents about carbon taxes, missing renewable energy, afforestation, and industrial processes. The expansion lacks breadth.
878.ap: AMD (Agent-Mediated Dialogic Framework) uses three specialized agents working together like a conversation. First, a Socratic Questioning Agent rephrases the initial query into three sub-questions, each inspired by a different angle (e.g., historical, technical, societal). For "climate solutions," it might ask "What are the historical approaches?", "What new technologies exist?", "What policy frameworks work?". Second, a Dialogic Answering Agent generates pseudo-answers to each sub-question, enriching the query with multiple perspectives. Third, a Reflective Feedback Agent evaluates which pseudo-answers are actually good and filters out the noisy ones. The three agents together refine the expansion iteratively.
878.ww: Why does this work? Multi-agent dialogue is inherently diverse. Each agent has a different role, so they push on the query from different angles. The Socratic dimension ensures breadth—it forces the system to think historically, technically, and societally, for instance. The feedback step acts as a quality gate, removing expansions that aren't coherent or relevant, keeping only the high-confidence additions. This is richer and more diverse than a single LLM making one pass.
878.po: Experiments on standard benchmarks (BEIR, TREC) show AMD expands queries better than prior LLM-based methods. The concrete payoff: when a user searches for something, the system retrieves more relevant documents because the query expansion is broader and more thoughtful, leading to better search results across the board.

879.bp: This is a vision statement rather than a research paper. The author is asking: what comes next after traditional recommendation and search systems? Foundation models (large, multimodal models that understand images, video, audio, and text) are now powerful enough to do more than spit out ranked lists. They can reason, understand context, and explain their reasoning. What if we combined that into a single personal assistant that discovers information, recommends, and helps you learn?
879.wh: The old systems (2000s-2010s) were specialized: a recommender system for products, a search engine for documents, a decision-support tool for analysis. Each solved one narrow problem. Now, foundation models can do many things at once. But the gap is in *personalization* and *alignment*: how do you make a single model that understands your preferences, your goals, your context, and your values? How do you ensure it reasons correctly and doesn't hallucinate? That's the unsolved problem.
879.ap: The paper sketches three trends to watch. First, moving from specialized systems to a single multimodal model that can see images, hear audio, watch video, and reason about all of it together. Second, fundamental research on *how to personalize* these models—how to make them genuinely adapt to individual users, not just serve generic recommendations. Third, combining "System 1" (fast, intuitive, pattern-based thinking) and "System 2" (slow, deliberate, reasoning-based thinking) into a single assistant that can both quickly recognize patterns and carefully reason through hard problems.
879.ww: The reasoning: current systems are fragmented (search vs. recommender vs. decision support), which creates friction. A truly universal assistant would integrate all three. By combining multimodal understanding with reasoning and personalization, you'd get a system that feels more like talking to a knowledgeable friend, not a machine serving ranked lists.
879.po: This is a research agenda, not a concrete product, but the payoff the author envisions is clear: a single AI assistant that can discover relevant information, recommend actions, explain reasoning, and adapt to the individual user, across all modalities (text, image, video, audio). This is aspirational and marks a shift in thinking from "build better recommenders" to "build better personal reasoning partners."

880.bp: Citation networks map how research papers reference each other, forming a web of knowledge. Scientists use these networks to trace ideas ("who cited who first?"), find related work, and assess influence. But citation networks are typically sparse in metadata—some papers have rich author affiliation data, some don't; some have keywords, some lack them. Richer metadata would make these networks more useful for discovery and clustering researchers. The question: can language models fill in the gaps?
880.wh: Citation metadata comes from publication metadata databases, but that metadata is incomplete or inconsistent across papers. One paper might list detailed author affiliations and keywords, while another is missing both. Using that incomplete data directly to analyze a citation network gives a distorted picture. You could try to fill gaps manually, but that's slow and expensive for millions of papers. Language models could do it automatically, but they can hallucinate—they might make up plausible-sounding but false information ("John Smith is from MIT" when he's actually from Stanford).
880.ap: The paper proposes using LLMs to generate factual descriptions for sparse metadata fields. For instance, if a paper has an incomplete author biography, the LLM writes a concise factual summary. These descriptions are then encoded into numbers using DeBERTa (another language model, used for compression). Those numerical representations become node features in a heterogeneous citation network—a graph where papers, authors, and venues are all nodes with rich features. To reduce hallucination, the authors used Chain-of-Thought prompting (asking the LLM to "think step-by-step" before generating answers) and evaluated the generated descriptions manually.
880.ww: Why does this help? Rich metadata allows citation networks to capture semantic meaning, not just citations. An author's description tells you what they work on, so you can find related researchers who've never cited each other (but should have). Better features lead to better author classification ("Is this author a machine learning researcher or a biologist?") and author clustering ("Which researchers are in the same field?"). The LLM does the annotation, so it scales to millions of papers.
880.po: Experiments show author classification improves by 2-4.5% and author clustering improves by 8.9-18.1% when using LLM-generated metadata, outperforming traditional hand-crafted features. The concrete payoff: researchers can discover collaborators and related work more effectively using richer, more complete citation networks.

881.bp: When you're asking a conversational AI a question in a multi-turn dialog, you're not just asking it to find a document—you're asking it to retrieve a *structured entity* from a knowledge graph (a database of connected concepts and facts) that's relevant to your context and your previous questions. For instance, if you ask "Which actor played Batman in the 2005 film?" the system needs to retrieve the entity "Christian Bale" from a knowledge graph that connects movies, actors, characters, and years. This is harder than it sounds in a conversational setting.
881.wh: Previous systems for entity retrieval weren't built for conversation. They assumed a single, context-free query. But in conversation, context matters: if you previously asked about "Christopher Nolan films," and now ask "Who directed that Batman movie?", the system should remember that you mean Nolan, not just any Batman movie. Also, knowledge graphs have structure—entities have types, properties, and neighbors. A naive system might only look at whether "Christian Bale" lexically matches your query, and miss the entity entirely if you phrase it differently.
881.ap: The paper introduces QBLink-KG, the first benchmark dataset for Conversational Entity Retrieval from Knowledge Graphs (CER-KG), adapted from conversational reading comprehension data. It then proposes two neural architectures. NACER aggregates lexical and semantic relevance signals from the local neighborhood of candidate entities (nearby entities in the graph). DRAGON (also described in this batch) improves on NACER by using graph convolution and self-attention to model fine-grained relationships across the sub-graph, explicitly accounting for dialog history.
881.ww: The reason structure-aware retrieval works: entities in knowledge graphs are not isolated; they're surrounded by related entities and properties that provide context. By modeling the local graph structure, the system can infer meaning. If "Batman" is connected to "Christian Bale" and "2005," and your dialog mentioned 2005, the system can make the connection. Graph convolution and self-attention let the model learn which neighbors and properties matter for a given query and dialog history.
881.po: The payoff is better conversational entity retrieval. In conversational AI systems—whether voice assistants or text-based chatbots—users can ask follow-up questions, and the system correctly retrieves the right entity from a knowledge graph, taking previous context into account. This feels more natural and less frustrating than systems that ignore context or miss entities.

882.bp: News recommendation systems suggest articles to readers. But text descriptions of news can be exaggerated or biased, which degrades recommendation quality. What if you also had the news image? A picture of a storm is more objective than a headline saying "Catastrophic flooding." This paper asks: can images help debias text, and can a language model learn to extract factual knowledge from text by being trained on text+image pairs, then later use just the text alone?
882.wh: Text-only news recommendation relies on extracting key facts from article text. But article text is often editorialized: "The devastating policy cut benefits" vs. the more neutral "Policy X reduced benefits by Y amount." A standard text processor can't easily separate fact from opinion. Images are harder to bias than words—a photograph of something happened, while words can spin it. But images aren't always available. The gap: can you use image+text pairs to teach a model to extract unbiased facts, then compress that knowledge into a text-only model so it works even when no image is available?
882.ap: IGKnow (Image-Guided Knowledge distillation framework) uses a large multimodal language model (one that reads both text and images) to extract factual triples (subject-relationship-object facts, like "Policy X reduced benefits by 5%") from articles that have both text and images. This multimodal model serves as a teacher. The factual triples are grounded in visual information, so they're less likely to be biased. Then, a text-only model is trained to reproduce those triples using only the article text. The paper also introduces TriSFT, a special training technique that makes the model robust to different orderings of facts (so it learns the facts, not their order).
882.ww: Why does this work? Multimodal learning acts as a debiasing signal. If text says "devastating" but the image shows moderate damage, the image ground truth wins. By extracting triples from this grounded source, you get cleaner facts. Then, compressing those facts into a text-only model is like asking: "Given only the text, how would you say these facts?" The model learns to focus on language that signals factuality, not emotional language. TriSFT prevents the model from memorizing the *order* of facts, forcing it to learn their meaning.
882.po: The payoff is better news recommendation. When the system uses these debiased, image-grounded facts for ranking articles, recommendations are more objective. Users see articles that match their interests based on actual content, not on emotionally charged language. Experiments in sequential news recommendation (where previous articles influence future suggestions) show that debiased triples improve recommendation quality.

883.bp: This is a workshop proposal, not a research paper. The organizers are hosting a forum to discuss how generative models (like ChatGPT) and large language models are changing recommendation and search systems. The underlying premise: these systems used to be built with traditional machine learning techniques (neural networks trained to predict clicks, ratings, etc.). Now, foundation models and generative systems have arrived, and the field needs to rethink everything.
883.wh: The old paradigm: build a model to predict the next item a user will click/buy. The new paradigm: generate personalized text, images, or recommendations on-the-fly using a foundation model. But there's a gap in the research community: academics are publishing in generative modeling, but only some of that research speaks directly to recommendation and search. Meanwhile, industry is rapidly deploying generative systems for recommendations. The workshop bridges that gap by bringing both communities together.
883.ap: The workshop focuses on the intersection of generative models and recommendation/search. Topics include how language models can be used for recommendation, how to personalize generative systems, how to combine traditional collaborative filtering (learning from user-item interactions) with generative understanding (understanding the meaning of items and users semantically). The event expects over 100 attendees from academia and industry.
883.ww: The reasoning: generative models can do things classical recommenders cannot—they can generate explanations, adapt on-the-fly to new users, understand semantic meaning. But they also have new risks (hallucination, bias, slower inference). The workshop exists to answer: what's the right way to combine classical and generative approaches for recommendation?
883.po: The payoff is a shared understanding across academia and industry about how generative AI is reshaping recommendation systems, and potentially new research directions and collaborations emerging from the cross-pollination of ideas.

884.bp: Many real-world prediction tasks involve regression on tabular data—predicting house prices, user engagement scores, revenue forecasts. These systems are deployed online, where they receive new data constantly. The problem: the distribution of incoming data can shift over time (a recession changes user behavior, a new competitor enters the market, a trend changes). A model trained on old data might perform terribly on new data. This paper asks: how do you adapt a regression model at inference time, without retraining, when the data distribution shifts?
884.wh: Existing approaches for handling distribution shift assume you know what the new distribution looks like, or that you can afford to retrain the model. But online systems don't have that luxury. You can't stop serving predictions while retraining. Also, in regression, a common challenge is data imbalance in the target: lots of easy predictions (predicting a price for a common item) and few hard predictions (predicting a price for a rare item). When distribution shifts *and* you have imbalance, the rare cases become even rarer in the new distribution, and the model falters.
884.ap: The paper proposes a two-part approach. First, a Region-Aware Mixture of Experts: use a Gaussian Mixture Model (a statistical technique) to identify distinct clusters or regions in the data. Train separate expert sub-models, each specialized to one region. Synthesize training data for rare regions so each expert gets enough examples. Second, Test-Time Self-Supervised Expert Aggregation: at inference time, don't use a fixed weighting of experts. Instead, look at each incoming test instance, figure out which region it belongs to, and dynamically upweight the expert trained for that region. This happens without retraining, just by adjusting how you combine expert predictions.
884.ww: Why does this work? By decomposing the problem into regions, each expert can optimize for its own regime. The Gaussian Mixture Model automatically finds where the data naturally clusters. At test time, adjusting expert weights on-the-fly means rare instances get the right specialist, not a model trained mostly on common cases. The self-supervised step uses only the features of the incoming test instance, not labels, so you can adapt without retraining.
884.po: The payoff is better regression performance when deployment distributions shift. For web applications—price prediction, engagement forecasting—this means the system stays accurate even as user behavior or the market changes. Real-world experiments on four datasets show this framework handles imbalanced regression under distribution shift significantly better than fixed models.
